note: These entries are heuristics for triage and training. They are not a mail-authentication oracle. A message can pass technical mail checks and still be fraud.

codes.meaning: The sender uses a free webmail domain instead of the partner domain you expect for business freight or payments.
The domain looks similar to one on file but is not an exact match. This is a spelling and typosquatting check, not proof of mail authenticity.
The text may use letters from another alphabet that look like normal Latin letters.
The message pushes speed, same-day action, or tells the reader not to call.
Banking, EFT, Interac, or other payment instructions appear in the request.
A value in the request does not match what your directory or TMS already stores.
The email domain is not the partner domain you have on file.
The message asks for a link click, sign-in, or sharing of access codes.
The message asks for remote access to plant, refrigeration, or OT-related systems.
A carrier or broker not on your approved list is being introduced for a load.
Dock, yard, or delivery destination may be changing away from the planned cold store or DC.
Bill of lading, proof of delivery, or seal details may be altered.
SupplyChek does not treat SPF, DKIM, or DMARC results as proof that a payment, dock, or access request is legitimate. A passing mail check is not proof the sender meant what the message says.
